title: Rental Scams in India: How They Work and How to Avoid Them
seoTitle: Rental Scams in India and How to Avoid Them
description: How rental scams in India actually work, the red flags that most reliably predict one, and the ownership checks to run before you transfer any money.
excerpt: Most landlords are not scammers. But rental fraud clusters exactly where you're most vulnerable — the urgent move, the listing that's slightly too good. Here's how to spot it and what to check before you pay.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: Renters who have been on the wrong end of a token advance

hero.alt: Futuristic illustration of a genuine listing staying solid under a jade shield of light while glitching duplicates dissolve behind it

faq.q: Is it normal to pay a token advance before seeing a flat in India?
faq.a: Token advances are a real convention, but they come after a viewing, not before one. Paying to hold a property you have never stood inside is the single most common way renters lose money. If a token is genuinely required, keep it small, pay it by bank transfer, and get a written acknowledgement naming the property and the owner.

faq.q: How do I check that someone actually owns the property they are renting out?
faq.a: Ask for the latest property tax receipt, a recent electricity bill in the owner’s name, or the sale deed for that address. Then check that the name on the document matches the name on the bank account you are paying and the name on the agreement. Genuine owners produce one of these without fuss because tenants have asked them before.

faq.q: Can I get my money back if I have been scammed on a rental?
faq.a: Sometimes, but honestly, often not. Report to your bank immediately and file on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal the same day, because funds transferred to a mule account are usually withdrawn within hours. People who recover money almost always reported within a day or two. Civil recovery of a small amount frequently costs more than the amount itself.

faq.q: Is it safe to rent a flat in another city without seeing it?
faq.a: It is the highest-risk way to rent, because every warning sign is harder to check from a distance. If you must, send someone you actually know to stand inside the property, insist on a live video call where you decide where the camera points, and pay nothing beyond a small documented amount until a person you trust has been physically inside.

faq.q: What is the single biggest red flag in a rental listing?
faq.a: Two, and they usually appear together: pressure to transfer money immediately, and a rent noticeably below everything comparable nearby. Urgency exists to stop you checking, and under-pricing is a volume tactic to generate enquiries. Either one on its own is a reason to slow down. Both together is a reason to walk away.

faq.q: The person showing me the flat says he is the owner’s relative. Is that a problem?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but it needs to be resolved before money moves. Ask for written authorisation from the owner and for a document proving who owns the property. Caretakers, relatives and previous tenants letting out a flat they have no right to let is one of the most common frauds, precisely because the flat itself is completely real.

body:
Meera nearly sent ₹25,000 to a stranger on a Tuesday afternoon.

She'd been flat-hunting in Pune for three weeks and was sick of it. Then a 2BHK in Baner turned up — bright photos, a balcony, ₹18,000 a month when everything else in that pocket was closer to thirty. She messaged. The reply came in four minutes, friendly and detailed, almost relieved to hear from her.

The owner was in Dubai on a work posting, he said. His caretaker held the keys. Four other people had asked about the flat that morning. A token of ₹25,000 would hold it until Saturday. Fully refundable, obviously.

She had the transfer screen open.

What stopped her was small and slightly random. She dropped one of the photos into a reverse image search, mostly out of curiosity about the floor tiles. The same kitchen came back on a listing in Hyderabad, posted eleven months earlier.

So she asked one more question. Could he send a copy of the last electricity bill?

He never replied again.

Meera lost nothing. She still calls it the closest she's come to losing a month's salary, and she is not a careless person. That's the part worth sitting with.

## Most landlords are not scammers. The few who are know where to stand.

Let's get this out of the way early, because fraud articles have a habit of turning readers into people who interrogate a retired schoolteacher about her sale deed.

The overwhelming majority of people renting out property in India are ordinary owners with one flat, or two, often bought as a retirement plan. They aren't running a scheme. They're mildly anxious about their tiles, they want the rent on time, and they'd quite like you to not put nails in the walls.

Rental fraud isn't everywhere. What it is, is *concentrated*. It clusters where you're least able to defend yourself: your first week in a new city, the move you had two weeks' notice for, the Sunday when you've seen four disappointing flats and this one has actual sunlight.

Scammers don't fish randomly. They fish where the pressure is.

## Why this works on smart people

The instinct is to assume victims were gullible. They mostly weren't.

**Search fatigue.** After twenty listings that looked nothing like their photos, a good one produces relief. Relief and scrutiny use the same muscle, and relief gets there first.

**Manufactured scarcity.** "Two other people are seeing it this evening" is the most effective sentence in the fraud vocabulary, because it's also true half the time in a real market. You can't tell the two apart from the sentence alone.

**The scam borrows the shape of a legitimate deal.** Owners genuinely do live abroad. Caretakers genuinely do hold keys. Token advances genuinely are a convention here. Nothing in the script is *inherently* absurd — that's the design. It's a normal transaction with one load-bearing part removed.

**The amount is calibrated.** Rarely ₹3 lakh. Usually ₹20,000, ₹35,000, one month's rent — big enough to be worth stealing, small enough that pursuing it costs more than it recovers.

And a quieter one: politeness. Asking a stranger to prove they own the thing they're standing in feels rude. Scammers rely on your manners more than your ignorance.

## The patterns, and what each one is actually after

### The token advance that evaporates

The classic. You're asked to transfer money to "hold" the flat — before a viewing, or straight after one, before anything is written down. Then they stop answering. Sometimes they stall a week first, which buys time to run the same script on four other people.

The tell is the sequence, not the amount. Money moving before a viewing, before an agreement, before you've verified anything — that's the whole scam in one step.

### Fake listings built from other people's photos

Photos get lifted from older listings, other cities, sometimes foreign property sites. The giveaway is often aesthetic: the kitchen is a little too Scandinavian, the light is wrong for India, the room has a radiator.

The rent is set below market on purpose. Not slightly — noticeably, because the point is volume. A cheap listing generates twenty enquiries where a fairly priced one generates two, and the fraudster only needs one person to transfer.

If a flat is priced far under everything comparable within a kilometre, that isn't a bargain. It's a filter, and it's filtering for you.

### The person showing the flat has no authority to let it

Subtler than the outright fake, and more common. The flat is real. The photos are real. You can walk around it. But the man with the keys is a watchman, a relative, a previous tenant, or a caretaker who decided the empty flat was an income opportunity while the owner is out of the country. He collects a deposit and a month's rent. Sometimes he even hands you keys. Then the owner turns up.

The question that breaks this — *who owns this flat, and can I see something in their name?* — takes eight seconds to ask, and almost nobody asks it.

### The same flat at three prices, from three different "agents"

You'll see it on any listing site: identical rooms, identical balcony, three prices, three phone numbers. Sometimes it's brokers competing over one property, which is annoying but legal. Sometimes one of the three is nobody at all.

Duplicates matter because they tell you nobody in that chain has a verified relationship with the property. Passed hand to hand until three people advertise it independently, the person you're talking to may be four steps from anyone who has met the owner.

### Visiting fees and "key deposits"

A caretaker asks ₹500 to show you the flat. A "manager" wants ₹2,000 as a refundable key deposit before a viewing. Small amounts, so people pay — and that's the model: ₹500 from thirty people a week, and nobody ever signs anything. It isn't always criminal fraud; sometimes it's just an unauthorised toll. Either way, paying to *look* at a property is not a normal cost of renting in India. Treat it as a stop sign, not an inconvenience.

### Sublet fraud

Someone rents a flat legitimately, then lets it to you with no right to do so. You pay a deposit to a person who is themselves a tenant. When the real owner finds out — and they do — you have no agreement with anyone who owns anything, and no standing to stay.

The uncomfortable version: the sub-letter may have been perfectly pleasant and may even have believed it was fine. Your loss is the same. It's one reason a written agreement naming the actual owner matters more than people think — worth reading [what a rental agreement should contain](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india) before you sign one.

### Deposit-farming landlords

Not a scam in the criminal sense, which is exactly why it's so durable. It's a business model. The flat is real, the owner is real, the agreement is real — but the deposit is six or eight months' rent and the owner has quietly decided that withholding a chunk of it is part of the yield. There's always a repaint, always a list, always a delay. Then the flat is re-let and it runs again.

You can't spot this from a listing. You can sometimes spot it by asking the outgoing tenant one question — *did you get your deposit back, and how long did it take?* — and by keeping the documentation habits in our piece on [getting a security deposit back](/blog/security-deposits-in-india).

### Renting sight-unseen from another city

Every pattern above gets worse when you're 900 kilometres away and starting a job on the first. The shape is consistent: contact stays on WhatsApp only, the "owner" is always travelling, video calls get postponed or are suspiciously short, and there's steady gentle pressure to transfer *today*. You're being asked to trust a photograph and a voice.

Relocating renters get targeted deliberately — a deadline, no local network, nobody's door to knock on. If you must rent remotely: send someone you actually know to stand in the flat, insist on a live walk-through where you choose where the camera points, and pay nothing beyond a small documented amount until someone you trust has been physically inside.

## Red flags, ranked by how reliably they predict a scam

Not all warning signs carry the same weight. Some are near-certainties; some are just Indian renting being itself.

| Red flag | What it usually means | How worried to be |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pressure to transfer money today | The oldest lever there is. Urgency exists to stop you checking. | Highest. Walk away. |
| Rent far below everything comparable nearby | Under-pricing is a volume tactic for fake listings. | Highest. Assume it's bait. |
| Money asked for before you've seen the flat | There is no legitimate version of this. | Very high |
| Refuses or deflects on proof of ownership | Either not the owner, or not authorised to let. | Very high |
| Owner "abroad", keys with a third party | Sometimes true. Also the standard script. | High — verify before anything moves |
| Cash only, or transfer to a name that isn't the owner's | Removes the trail on purpose. | High |
| Same flat listed at several prices by several people | Nobody in the chain has a verified relationship with it. | Medium-high |
| "Visiting fee" or key deposit to view | An unauthorised toll at best. | Medium-high |
| WhatsApp-only, no calls, no meeting | Consistent with running many marks at once. | Medium-high |
| Photos that look imported or oddly professional | Lifted images. Reverse-search them. | Medium |
| Won't put anything in writing | Could be laziness. Could be a reason. | Medium |
| Broker vague about who the owner is | Very common, not always sinister. | Low-medium |

The top two carry most of the predictive weight. **Urgency and an unusually low price** are the signals that most reliably mean you're being worked. Almost everything else is a reason to slow down and ask a question; those two are a reason to leave.

## The verification playbook

Half an hour, spread across a viewing and one evening. It eliminates almost every pattern above.

**1. Verify ownership, not identity.** A photo ID proves someone is who they say. It doesn't prove they own a flat. Ask for any one of these, in the name of the person receiving your money:

- The latest **property tax receipt** for that address
- A recent **electricity bill** in the owner's name
- The **sale deed** or, in some states, the khata / Index II / mutation record

You aren't being paranoid. Genuine owners produce one without fuss, often before you ask, because they've been asked before. Someone who bristles at the question is telling you something.

**2. Match the name to the account.** The name on that document should match the bank account you're transferring to and the name on the agreement. If those three aren't the same person, you need written authorisation — a power of attorney, a signed letter. "He's my brother-in-law, it's fine" isn't one.

**3. Meet at the property, in daylight, with the owner there at least once.** Not a café. Not a broker's office. If the owner is genuinely abroad, get a video call from inside the flat where you direct the camera. A scammer can send a two-minute clip; they can't take you on a tour you're steering.

**4. Reverse-image-search the photos.** Thirty seconds. If the same rooms turn up in another city or another year, you're done.

**5. Talk to somebody who isn't selling you the flat.** The watchman. The neighbour on that floor. Ask who owns it and who lived there before. That one habit destroys sublet and caretaker fraud for the price of a two-minute conversation.

**6. Never pay before you've read the agreement.** In full, at home, before any money moves. If the answer is "we'll do the agreement after the token", you've found the scam. Our [questions to ask before you commit to a rental](/blog/questions-to-ask-before-renting) covers this stage, and our [house-hunting checklist](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india) folds it into the rest of the process.

**7. Pay by bank transfer, always.** UPI, NEFT, IMPS, cheque — anything with a date, an amount and a named recipient. Cash leaves you nothing to show a bank, a police station or a court.

**8. Sanity-check the price yourself.** Look at what similar flats on the same streets actually cost. A map answers this faster than a list — [seeing where homes sit relative to each other](/blog/why-maps-beat-lists-for-finding-a-home) makes an outlier obvious in a way a sorted column doesn't.

**9. Keep everything.** Listing screenshots, the chat thread, the phone number, the payment reference, the documents you were shown. If anything goes wrong, that's your entire case.

## If you've already paid

First: it happens to careful people, and beating yourself up isn't a step in the process. Move fast instead — speed is the only variable you still control.

**1. Contact your bank immediately.** If the transfer is very recent there is sometimes — not often — a window to flag it before the account is emptied. Ask them to record a fraud complaint against the beneficiary account and get a reference number.

**2. Put the demand in writing.** Message or email the person: the amount, the date, what it was for, and that you require it returned by a specific date. Factual, unemotional. Less about persuading them than about creating a document that exists.

**3. File on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal** at [cybercrime.gov.in](https://cybercrime.gov.in/) if any part of it happened online — which, given the listing and the transfer, it almost certainly did. Reporting fast genuinely matters for any chance of freezing funds.

**4. File a police complaint at the station covering the property's area.** Take printouts of everything and ask for written acknowledgement. If they're reluctant to register an FIR, the portal complaint gives you a parallel timestamped record.

**5. Report the listing** wherever you found it, so the same photos aren't used on the next person.

Now the honest part, because this article is worth nothing without it: **recovery is often poor.** Money moved to a mule account is frequently withdrawn within hours. Investigations across state lines are slow. Civil recovery of ₹30,000 can cost more than ₹30,000. Some people do get their money back, usually because they reported within a day or two while the account was still funded. Many don't.

That asymmetry is exactly why half an hour of verification beats any remedy afterwards. And if you're in a dispute with a landlord rather than a fraudster — a withheld deposit, an eviction threat — that's different ground, and [what tenants can actually enforce](/blog/tenant-rights-in-india) is the more useful reading.

## What StayOnMap does about this, and where we stop

Careful here, because a platform claiming it prevents fraud would be doing what the scammers do: sounding more certain than the facts allow.

**We cannot prevent fraud.** We can't verify that every person on the platform is who they say they are, and anybody who tells you they can is selling something.

What we've done is close some of the gaps fraud lives in. Rent, deposit and maintenance are required fields on every listing, so the price is stated up front and can't be revised upward in a stairwell. There's no brokerage, which removes one opaque payment. You contact the owner directly instead of through a chain of intermediaries — which matters, because most patterns above depend on distance between you and whoever owns the flat. Every listing has a report button, and we run duplicate detection.

We do have owner verification. It's real, but know what it is: an admin reading submitted documents and making a judgement. A signal, not a guarantee — we'd rather say that plainly than let a badge do work it can't do.

So the playbook above still applies here. Ask for the property tax receipt. Meet at the flat. Pay by bank transfer.

## What to remember

Rental fraud in India isn't an epidemic and isn't rare enough to ignore. It's targeted, and it targets urgency.

Two signals carry most of the weight: someone pushing you to transfer money today, or a rent well below everything comparable nearby. Treat either as the end of the conversation rather than a question to resolve.

Verify ownership, not identity. A property tax receipt or an electricity bill in the owner's name, matching the account you're paying into, closes off most of this article in one step.

And never let money move before you've read the agreement and stood inside the flat. Every scam here needs that one thing to happen out of order.

Meera found a place six weeks later. Smaller, more expensive, in a building where the watchman knew the owner's family by name. She asked for the electricity bill anyway. The owner laughed and sent it in about ninety seconds — because she'd been asked before, by tenants who learned the same lesson the harder way.
